newsitem.title: USA: Bundesbank's Issing warns unions face tough EMU ride.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank's Issing warns unions face tough EMU ride.

text.p: Wage policy negotiotors face tough times ahead due to the transition to a single currency in Europe, but their actions will play a decisive role in the euro's success, Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said.

Speaking at a forum on Washington on Monday afternoon, Issing said the wage transparency created by a single currency area would naturally put negotiators under pressure to bring their pay levels in line with that of other countries.

"The difficulties with which wage negotiators will be faced in the monetary union should not be underrated," Issing said. "The exchange rate illusion will no longer exist. Wage differentials will become more transparent. Judging by past experiences this will trigger pressure for adjustment."
Major policy errors in this area could undermine the stability and crediblity of the European currency, he added.
Issing's remarks come against a backdrop of rumbling industrial unrest in Germany and France, the two countries at the heart of Europe's integration plans.
In Germany, over 120,000 workers took to the streets on Tuesday to protest against a new law that cuts worker's sick pay to 80 percent of the normal pay level from 100 percent.

And while France is not expecting a repeat of the strikes that crippled public services for four weeks last November, unions there plan widespread walk-outs to protest against cutbacks in the public sector and reinforce wage demands.

The industrial action reflects unpopular measures taken to lick Europe's public budgets into shape ahead of monetary union and to iron out inflexibilities in labour markets that make European locations less attractive as a production site.

Countries wanting to join the new euro from 1999 must meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and debt in 1997, with the fiscal targets proving the hardest to match for almost all nations.

While industrialists and governments are optimistic that the euro will reduce Europe's high structural unemployment in the longer term, the unions argue that austerity policies mean EMU is being bought at the expense of society's weakest.

Issing warned that this conflict between the traditional goals of trade unions and the need to shape European labour markets to counter global competition would become even more intense in the single currency environment.
A leveling-off of wages throughout the currency area would be inflationary unless matched by gains in productivity, Issing said, adding such gains were unlikely.
The alternative route, "a Europeanisation of wage policy so that uniform pay rises are agreed within the common currency area," would be equally disastrous, he said.
"That would not only lock in existing wage differences but also preclude from the outset the appropriate response to the concrete labour market situation of the respective sector or region," he said.

Karl-Heinz Wessel, president of the German banking association, said in answer to a question that the unions would of course fight any loss of benefits which had been hard won in negotiations over the years.
But he agreed that such change was essential.
"It is very difficult to scroll back benefits which have been driven so high by wage policies," he said. "It affects every individual and is thus hard to change."
But Issing warned that reform of welfare systems, which would inevitably mean losses for some individuals, was unavoidable if the Euro economic area was to be competitive.

"Calls to supplement monetary union by social union ---- harmonisation at the highest possible level -- are on the wrong track," he said. "Monetary union requires the opposite -- considerably more flexibility in the labour market."
